- [Basic payment](/docs/payments/send-basic-payment): the single-transfer endpoint.
- [Payment with memo](/docs/payments/send-payment-with-memo): the memo field used above to tag a run.
- [Indexing and reconciliation](/docs/payments/accept-indexing): the same list endpoint, used for inbound transfers.
- [Manage API keys](/docs/developing-with-sdp/manage-api-keys#allowed-operations): limit a payout key to payments.
- [Idempotency](/docs/developing-with-sdp/idempotency): how replays resolve.

---

### Recurring payments
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/payments/recurring-payments

> Pay a counterparty a fixed amount on a schedule from an SDP custody wallet, with SDP signing and collecting each payment.

A **recurring payment** sends a fixed amount of one token from one of your custody wallets to one counterparty account, once per period. Your SDP custody wallet is the payer. SDP signs every transaction with it and collects each payment when it falls due. Use it for payroll, retainers, vendor payments, or any other outgoing schedule you control.

Recurring payments are built on the Solana Subscriptions program. When you activate one, SDP creates a plan owned by your source wallet and authorizes a subscription to it from that same wallet. Each collection is a pull under that subscription, signed by the source wallet. That's why a recurring payment record carries `planId`, `subscriptionId`, `planPda` and `subscriptionPda`.

## Prerequisites

- A custody wallet to pay from, with a custody signer configured, holding the token. You pass its SDP Wallet `id` (`cwlt_…`, from `GET /v1/wallets`) as `sourceCustodyWalletId`. The provider `walletId`, the wallet address and the legacy `sourceWalletId` selector are not accepted.
- An `active` counterparty with an `active` counterparty account of kind `crypto_wallet` on `solana`. See `POST /v1/counterparties/{counterpartyId}/accounts`.
- A supported token: a USD stablecoin that SDP recognizes on your project's network, such as `USDC`, or a token issued in this project whose status is `active`. Native SOL is not supported.
- An API key with the permissions listed under [Permissions](#permissions), whose `payments:write` wallet scope includes the source wallet.

## Lifecycle

1. **Create** the schedule. SDP stores it as `pending_activation`; nothing happens on-chain yet.
2. **Activate** it. SDP creates the on-chain plan and subscription, signed by your source wallet, and the schedule becomes `active` with a `nextCollectionDueAt`.
3. **Collect.** SDP's background job collects each payment once it's due. You can also start a due collection yourself with `collect`.
4. **Update, cancel or resume** the schedule as needed.

## Create a schedule

`POST /v1/payments/recurring-payments` takes:

| Field | Required | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `sourceCustodyWalletId` | Yes | SDP Wallet `id` (`cwlt_…`) that funds every payment. |
| `counterpartyId` | Yes | The counterparty being paid. Must be `active`. |
| `counterpartyAccountId` | Yes | That counterparty's `crypto_wallet` account. Must be `active`. Payments go to its Solana wallet address. |
| `token` | Yes | A supported stablecoin symbol or mint, or the mint of a token issued in this project. Stored as the mint address. |
| `amount` | Yes | Amount per payment, as a positive decimal string in UI units. |
| `periodHours` | Yes | Whole hours between payments, from 1 to 8760. For example `24` (daily), `168` (weekly) or `720` (every 30 days). Periods are fixed lengths, not calendar months. |
| `firstCollectionAt` | No | ISO 8601 timestamp, which must be in the future. If you leave it out, the first payment is due one period after activation. |
| `metadataUri` | No | `http` or `https` URL, up to 128 characters, stored with the on-chain plan. |

Unknown fields are rejected with `400`.

<Tabs items={["curl", "TypeScript", "Java"]}>
<Tab value="curl">
```bash title="Terminal"
curl -X POST https://api.solana.com/v1/payments/recurring-payments \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sk_test_..." \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "sourceCustodyWalletId": "cwlt_123",
    "counterpartyId": "cpty_4837",
    "counterpartyAccountId": "counterparty_account_4837",
    "token": "USDC",
    "amount": "2500.00",
    "periodHours": 720,
    "firstCollectionAt": "2026-06-01T09:00:00Z"
  }'
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="TypeScript">
```typescript title="create-recurring-payment.ts"
const response = await fetch(
  "https://api.solana.com/v1/payments/recurring-payments",
  {
    method: "POST",
    headers: {
      "Authorization": "Bearer sk_test_...",
      "Content-Type": "application/json",
    },
    body: JSON.stringify({
      sourceCustodyWalletId: "cwlt_123",
      counterpartyId: "cpty_4837",
      counterpartyAccountId: "counterparty_account_4837",
      token: "USDC",
      amount: "2500.00",
      periodHours: 720,
      firstCollectionAt: "2026-06-01T09:00:00Z",
    }),
  }
);
const { data } = await response.json();
// data.recurringPayment.id      — "prp_..."
// data.recurringPayment.status  — "pending_activation"
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="Java">
```java title="CreateRecurringPayment.java"
HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder()
    .uri(URI.create("https://api.solana.com/v1/payments/recurring-payments"))
    .header("Authorization", "Bearer sk_test_...")
    .header("Content-Type", "application/json")
    .POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString("""
        {
          "sourceCustodyWalletId": "cwlt_123",
          "counterpartyId": "cpty_4837",
          "counterpartyAccountId": "counterparty_account_4837",
          "token": "USDC",
          "amount": "2500.00",
          "periodHours": 720,
          "firstCollectionAt": "2026-06-01T09:00:00Z"
        }"""))
    .build();
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>

A `201` returns the stored schedule. The on-chain fields stay `null` until activation:

```json title="response.json"
{
  "data": {
    "recurringPayment": {
      "id": "prp_...",
      "sourceCustodyWalletId": "cwlt_123",
      "sourceProviderWalletId": "privy_wallet_123",
      "sourceAddress": "5aBCd...2eFg",
      "counterpartyId": "cpty_4837",
      "counterpartyAccountId": "counterparty_account_4837",
      "destinationAddress": "7xKXz...9fGh",
      "destinationTokenAccount": null,
      "token": "4zMMC9srt5Ri5X14GAgXhaHii3GnPAEERYPJgZJDncDU",
      "amount": "2500.00",
      "periodHours": 720,
      "firstCollectionAt": "2026-06-01T09:00:00.000Z",
      "nextCollectionDueAt": null,
      "planId": null,
      "subscriptionId": null,
      "status": "pending_activation"
    }
  },
  "meta": { "requestId": "req_...", "timestamp": "2026-05-14T09:00:00.000Z" }
}
```

The example is trimmed; see the [Payments API reference](/docs/reference/api/payments) for every field.

Create doesn't use the `Idempotency-Key` header, so retrying a create that timed out can leave you with two schedules. Before you retry, check with `GET /v1/payments/recurring-payments?counterpartyId=…`.

If your key carries allowed operations, they must include the create. See [Allowed operations](#allowed-operations).

## Activate

Activation takes no body:

```bash title="Terminal"
curl -X POST https://api.solana.com/v1/payments/recurring-payments/prp_abc123/activate \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sk_test_..."
```

SDP signs two steps with the source wallet: creating the on-chain plan, then authorizing the subscription. When the call returns `200`, both exist on-chain and the response shows `status: "active"` with `nextCollectionDueAt`, `planPda`, `planCreationSignature`, `subscriptionPda` and `authorizationSignature` filled in.

The first payment is due at `firstCollectionAt` if you set one, or one period after activation if you didn't. Always read the due date from `nextCollectionDueAt`.

- If activation fails, the schedule goes back to `pending_activation` and you can call `activate` again.
- Calling `activate` on a schedule that's already `active` returns it unchanged.
- While an activation is in progress, a second call returns `409`. If an activation stays in `activating` for 15 minutes, SDP's background job picks it up again, and you can call `activate` again yourself.

## Collection

### Automatic collection

SDP's background job collects every `active` schedule whose `nextCollectionDueAt` has passed. You don't need to call anything. The payment goes from the source wallet to the counterparty's associated token account for the token. SDP creates that account if it doesn't exist, and SDP's fee payer covers the network fee and the account rent.

Once SDP confirms the payment on-chain, `nextCollectionDueAt` moves forward by `periodHours` from the previous due date, not from the time of collection, so the schedule doesn't drift.

If an automatic collection fails, the job tries that due date again on a later run, no sooner than 30 minutes after the failure.

If SDP won't start new payments for the organization when a collection falls due, because the organization is suspended or deleted or production isn't enabled for a production project, the job records a `skipped` attempt with the reason in `error` and moves `nextCollectionDueAt` to the next due date after the current time. A skipped due date isn't collected later.

### Collect manually

`POST /v1/payments/recurring-payments/{id}/collect` starts the collection for the current due date straight away, for example to retry after you've topped up the source wallet:

```bash title="Terminal"
curl -X POST https://api.solana.com/v1/payments/recurring-payments/prp_abc123/collect \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sk_test_..."
```

```json title="response.json"
{
  "data": {
    "recurringPayment": { "id": "prp_...", "status": "active", "nextCollectionDueAt": "2026-07-01T09:00:00.000Z" },
    "collectionAttempt": {
      "id": "psca_...",
      "subscriptionId": "psub_...",
      "transferId": "xfr_...",
      "amount": "2500.00",
      "dueAt": "2026-06-01T09:00:00.000Z",
      "status": "confirmed",
      "signature": "3vZq...",
      "error": null,
      "metadata": { "source": "linked_transfer", "initialSource": "manual", "recurringPaymentId": "prp_...", "transferId": "xfr_...", "initiatedByKeyId": "key_..." }
    },
    "transfer": { "id": "xfr_...", "kind": "recurring_pay", "status": "confirmed", "amount": "2500.00", "signature": "3vZq..." }
  },
  "meta": { "requestId": "req_...", "timestamp": "2026-06-01T09:00:04.000Z" }
}
```

- Before `nextCollectionDueAt`, `collect` returns `400`.
- If the schedule isn't `active`, or a collection for this due date is already in progress, it returns `409`.
- Manual collection doesn't wait out the 30-minute retry delay that applies to automatic retries.
- If SDP can't confirm the submission straight away, the `200` returns the transfer as `processing` with its signature. Reconciliation settles it, and `nextCollectionDueAt` only moves forward after exact on-chain confirmation. Don't collect that due date again.

SDP keeps at most one in-flight or confirmed collection attempt per due date, so repeated `collect` calls for the same cycle don't pay twice.

### Collection attempts and transfers

Each collection creates a **collection attempt** for its due date and a payment transfer with `kind: "recurring_pay"`. To see the attempts for a schedule, pass its `subscriptionId` to the subscriptions endpoint:

```bash title="Terminal"
curl "https://api.solana.com/v1/payments/subscriptions/psub_abc123/collection-attempts?status=failed" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sk_test_..."
```

The response lists `collectionAttempts` with `total`, `page` and `pageSize`. Each attempt has:

- `status`: `processing`, `confirmed`, `failed` or `skipped` (the enum also has `pending`).
- `dueAt`: the due date it collects.
- `transferId` and `signature`: the linked transfer and on-chain transaction.
- `error`: the reason a failed attempt failed.
- `metadata.source`: `manual` or `automated` while it runs, `linked_transfer` once it's confirmed, or `retry` after a failure, with `metadata.retryAfterAt` and `metadata.initialSource`.

The transfers also appear in `GET /v1/payments/transfers`, for example filtered by `counterpartyId`.

## Update a schedule

`PATCH /v1/payments/recurring-payments/{id}` changes a schedule in `pending_activation` or `active`. Send only the fields you're changing; at least one is required. If you change `counterpartyId`, also send `counterpartyAccountId`.

- **Pending schedules** are updated directly. `firstCollectionAt` can only be changed here; send `null` to clear it.
- **Active schedules**: `metadataUri` and `nextCollectionDueAt` are updated in place. Changing `amount`, `periodHours`, `token`, `sourceCustodyWalletId`, `counterpartyId` or `counterpartyAccountId` makes SDP create and authorize a replacement on-chain subscription, cancel the old one, and switch the schedule over.
- `nextCollectionDueAt` can only be changed after activation. It can't be earlier than the next eligible collection (`400`); send `null` to reset it to the earliest eligible time.
- To change the source wallet, your key needs `payments:write` on both the old and the new wallet.

While the update runs, the schedule is `updating` and isn't collected, and another `PATCH` returns `409`. If an update is interrupted, the schedule stays `updating`. After 15 minutes, send the same `PATCH` again to finish it; a different body returns `409`.

## Cancel and resume

```bash title="Terminal"
curl -X POST https://api.solana.com/v1/payments/recurring-payments/prp_abc123/cancel \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sk_test_..."
```

- **Cancel** stops future collections. For an `active` schedule, SDP submits the on-chain cancellation (`canceling`, then `canceled`). A collection that's already processing may still settle. A schedule that was never activated is marked `canceled` without any on-chain step.
- **Resume** (`POST /v1/payments/recurring-payments/{id}/resume`) submits the on-chain resume for a `canceled` schedule that was activated before, and returns it to `active` (through `resuming`). Check `nextCollectionDueAt` in the response.

Both calls take no body. Calling either on a schedule already in the target state returns it unchanged. While one is in progress, a second call returns `409`. If a schedule stays in `canceling` or `resuming` for 15 minutes, SDP's background job finishes the operation.

## List and read

- `GET /v1/payments/recurring-payments` lists schedules, filtered by `counterpartyId` and `status`, with `page` and `pageSize` (up to 100). The response has `recurringPayments`, `total`, `page` and `pageSize`. It only includes schedules whose source wallet your key can read.
- `GET /v1/payments/recurring-payments/{id}` returns one schedule.

## Statuses

| Status | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `pending_activation` | Created; nothing on-chain yet. Can be updated, activated or canceled. |
| `activating` | Activation is in progress. |
| `active` | Collected when due. Can be updated, collected manually or canceled. |
| `updating` | An update is in progress. Not collected until it finishes. |
| `canceling` | Cancellation is in progress. |
| `canceled` | No further collections. Can be resumed if it was activated. |
| `resuming` | Resume is in progress. |
| `paused`, `expired` | Not collected. Update, cancel and resume return `409`. |

Only `active` schedules are collected.

## Allowed operations

If your key carries [allowed operations](/docs/developing-with-sdp/manage-api-keys#allowed-operations), three routes check them before SDP validates the request body:

| Operation type | Route |
| --- | --- |
| `recurring_payment_create` | `POST /v1/payments/recurring-payments` |
| `recurring_payment_update` | `PATCH /v1/payments/recurring-payments/{id}` |
| `recurring_payment_collection` | `POST /v1/payments/recurring-payments/{id}/collect` |

The `payment` family covers all three. If the key's list includes neither the family nor the route's operation type, the request returns `403` with `error.code: "OPERATION_NOT_ALLOWED"`: create stores no schedule, update changes nothing, and `collect` starts no collection. Activate, cancel and resume don't check the list.

Automatic collections run in SDP's background job, not under an API key, so allowed operations don't apply to them. Narrowing the list on the key that created a schedule doesn't stop its collections. Cancel the schedule to stop them.

## Errors

| Status | Typical causes |
| --- | --- |
| `400` | Invalid body: unknown field, unsupported token, `firstCollectionAt` not in the future, `periodHours` out of range. Counterparty or account not `active`, or account not `crypto_wallet`. `collect` before the due date. `nextCollectionDueAt` too early, `firstCollectionAt` after activation, or `nextCollectionDueAt` before activation. |
| `403` | The key lacks a permission or wallet scope, or (`OPERATION_NOT_ALLOWED`) its allowed operations don't include the operation. |
| `404` | Schedule, counterparty or counterparty account not found. |
| `409` | The operation isn't allowed from the current status, another operation on the schedule is in progress, or a collection for this due date is already processing. |

## Permissions

| Endpoint | Permissions |
| --- | --- |
| `POST /v1/payments/recurring-payments` | `payments:write`, `wallets:read`, `counterparties:read` |
| `PATCH /v1/payments/recurring-payments/{id}` | `payments:write`, `wallets:read`, `counterparties:read` |
| `POST /v1/payments/recurring-payments/{id}/activate`, `/cancel`, `/resume`, `/collect` | `payments:write`, `wallets:read` |
| `GET /v1/payments/recurring-payments`, `GET /v1/payments/recurring-payments/{id}` | `payments:read` |

Every write also needs the key's `payments:write` wallet scope to include the source wallet. See [Manage API keys](/docs/developing-with-sdp/manage-api-keys).

## Related

- [Payouts and disbursements](/docs/payments/send-payouts): one-off payments to many counterparties.
- [Manage API keys](/docs/developing-with-sdp/manage-api-keys#allowed-operations): limit a key to the operations it may perform.
- [Wallet balances](/docs/wallet-operations/balances): keep the source wallet funded.

## Payments — Accept Payments

### Accept payments
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/payments/accept-overview

> Receiving-address convention, integration options, and how to track inbound payments with SDP.

SDP does not ship a hosted checkout primitive. To accept payments, you publish a Solana address you control and detect inbound transfers via the SDP transfer list — this page covers the pattern; [verification](/docs/payments/accept-verification) and [indexing](/docs/payments/accept-indexing) cover the details.

## Receiving-address convention

The receiving address is a custody wallet you control. Two scopings to choose between:

- **One wallet per order** *(recommended for accept flows)* — provision a fresh custody wallet (or sub-account) per order or per customer and use the destination address itself as the correlation key. The inbound transfer's `destination` field maps 1:1 to your order row, so you do not depend on memo or reference fields that SDP does not surface for inbound payments.
- **One wallet per merchant scope** — for marketplaces, one custody wallet per seller; for treasury operations, one per ledger account. Reasonable when correlation isn't required (treasury, settlement) or when you accept a single fixed-amount payment per merchant.

The address you publish is the on-chain `address` of the custody wallet. Fetch it with [`GET /v1/wallets/{walletId}`](/docs/reference/api/wallets); when you only need wallet metadata, add `?includeBalance=false` to avoid a balance RPC and pricing lookup. You publish that address; senders use it as the destination of a normal SPL token transfer. SDP indexes the inbound transfer and exposes it in [`GET /v1/payments/transfers`](/docs/payments/accept-indexing) with `direction=inbound`.

**Correlation caveats.** For *customer-initiated* inbound transfers, SDP today does **not** populate `Transfer.memo` (Solana memo-program instructions aren't extracted into the record) and does **not** expose a reference field on the inbound record. The reliable on-record correlation key is the inbound transfer's `destination` — hence the per-order receiving-address recommendation. If you need memo- or reference-based correlation (e.g., for a Solana Pay URL that carries an order pubkey), read the on-chain transaction directly via Solana RPC using the transfer's `signature`.

## Integration options

There are two ways customers can land a payment on the address you control:

1. **Direct address share** — you display the address (and the expected token + amount) in your UI. The customer's wallet sends a transfer. This works with any Solana wallet and any client; SDP picks the transfer up purely from the on-chain side. Best for B2B settlement, treasury operations, and crypto-native flows.
2. **Solana Pay request** — for consumer checkout, you give the customer a [Solana Pay](https://solana.com/docs/payments/accept-payments/solana-pay) URL or QR code with the destination, amount, and a per-order `reference` pubkey. The customer's wallet builds the transfer and attaches the `reference` account on-chain, so you can match the transfer back to the order by reading the transaction directly via Solana RPC (the `reference` won't be on the SDP `Transfer` record — neither will any memo the wallet sets, since SDP doesn't extract memo-program instructions for inbound transfers). SDP does not ship a hosted Solana Pay endpoint or attach a Solana Pay reference on-chain today (see [Indexing and reconciliation → Solana Pay reference accounts](/docs/payments/accept-indexing#solana-pay-reference-accounts-roadmap)). For SDP-side correlation today, use **per-order destination addresses** (covered above); use the on-chain transaction (via RPC) when you need to read memo or `reference`.

## What SDP gives you today

- **Indexed inbound transfers** — `GET /v1/payments/transfers?direction=inbound` returns persisted transfers across your custody wallets. Filter by exact `custodyWalletId`; add `includeObserved=true` to include recent chain observations for that wallet. See [Indexing and reconciliation](/docs/payments/accept-indexing).
- **Per-transfer status reads** — `GET /v1/payments/transfers/{id}` for a single payment's lifecycle. See [Verifying a payment](/docs/payments/accept-verification).
- **Transaction history** — `GET /v1/transactions` lists past payments and issuance transactions in one feed, with cursor pagination and search by ID or signature. It covers persisted records only, not observed on-chain activity. See [Transaction history](/docs/payments/transactions).
- **Wallet balances** — `GET /v1/payments/wallets/{walletId}/balances` for the current per-token balance on a receiving wallet. See [Wallet balances](/docs/wallet-operations/balances).
- **Address-based correlation** — the inbound transfer's `destination` is the on-record correlation key for accept flows. Pair with per-order receiving addresses (see above) to map inbound transfers to orders without depending on memo. `Transfer.memo` is populated only for SDP-initiated transfers (outbound or internal); for customer-initiated inbound transfers the field is **omitted** from the response (it's optional in the schema, not nullable). Read the on-chain transaction via Solana RPC if you need memo or Solana Pay reference correlation.

## What SDP does not give you yet

- **No checkout session / payment intent object** — you do not pre-register an expected payment with the API. Inbound transfers are recognized after the fact by matching the on-record `destination` (token and amount are available for additional sanity checks). Memo and Solana Pay reference aren't on the transfer record for customer-initiated inbound transfers — see the [correlation caveats](#receiving-address-convention) above; read those from the on-chain transaction via Solana RPC if you need them.
- **No webhooks on settlement** — status changes are observed by polling `GET /v1/payments/transfers/{id}` or by re-listing with date filters. See the [polling cadence guidance](/docs/payments/accept-verification#polling-cadence).
- **No hosted Solana Pay URL endpoint** — if you want to ship a Solana Pay URL or QR, build it client-side from the destination address, token mint, amount, and reference pubkey.

## Worked example: a marketplace checkout

A minimum-viable accept flow built on the per-order-address pattern:

1. At checkout, provision (or claim from a warm pool) a **fresh custody wallet** for the order and stage an `orders` row with that wallet's on-chain address, the expected amount, and the token.
2. Display the per-order custody-wallet address, the token, and the amount to the customer. Build a Solana Pay URL from those fields if you want a QR code; no SDP-specific endpoint required.
3. The customer's wallet submits the transfer.
4. Your reconciliation worker periodically lists recent persisted inbound transfers. If it must discover chain activity not yet persisted, poll each receiving wallet with its exact `custodyWalletId` and `includeObserved=true`. Match each transfer's `destination` to an open order in your `orders` table.
5. When a match lands, mark the order paid and ship the goods. Use the transfer's `signature` (UNIQUE on the transfer record once present) to dedup if the worker is re-run.

This is intentionally low-level — there is no SDP-provided session object. Treat the `orders` table as your checkout state machine and SDP as the settlement and status backend.

## Next steps

- [Verifying a payment](/docs/payments/accept-verification) — status semantics and how to know when a payment is safe to act on.
- [Indexing and reconciliation](/docs/payments/accept-indexing) — listing inbound transfers, deduping, and building a delta-poll worker.

### Verifying a payment
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/payments/accept-verification

> Transfer-status semantics, finality on Solana, and recommended polling cadence for SDP transfers.

When a payment lands on a wallet you control, the inbound transfer moves through a handful of status states. This page describes those states, what each one means about on-chain finality, and how to decide when it is safe to ship goods or release funds.

## Status lifecycle

The `status` field on the `Transfer` record takes one of several values, depending on whether the transfer is a wallet transfer or a ramp transfer.

**Wallet transfers** (`POST /v1/payments/transfers`, and inbound transfers discovered on-chain):

| Status | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `processing` | The transfer is in flight. For outbound transfers this is the **initial state** at record creation: the transaction is being built and submitted; `signature` is not yet populated. |
| `confirmed` | The cluster has confirmed the transaction. `signature` and `slot` are populated. `blockTime` may also be set, but is not guaranteed at this stage — treat it as optional until `finalized`. |
| `finalized` | The slot containing the transaction is locked in — finality at the Solana cluster's strongest guarantee. `signature` and `slot` are populated; `blockTime` is best-effort and may remain `null` for transfers finalized by the `track-pending-transfers` job (which updates status and slot but does not backfill block time). Resolve a definitive timestamp from `signature` via Solana RPC if you need one. Safe to treat as irreversible. |
| `failed` | The transaction was built and submitted but rejected by the network (insufficient funds, frozen account, expired blockhash, etc.). The `error` field describes what reached the chain. |

Outbound wallet transfers move `processing → confirmed → finalized`. Inbound transfers discovered via on-chain signature history surface directly at `confirmed` (or `failed`) — they never appear as `processing`.

**Ramp transfers** (created by a [Ramp Quote](/docs/payments/ramps)):

| Status | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `pending` | The quote was created; no funding has been detected yet. No `signature`. |
| `awaiting_payment` | The quote's delivery mode is `manual_instructions` — SDP is waiting for the payer to fund the account described in the quote. |
| `settling` | The provider has detected or started processing the payment. |
| `completed` | The provider reports the ramp settled. |
| `canceled` | The ramp was canceled from the SDP dashboard before it was funded. |
| `expired` | The funding window elapsed without payment. |
| `failed` | The provider rejected or reversed the ramp. The `error` field describes why, when set. |

Any state can transition to `failed`; `failed`, `completed`, `canceled`, and `expired` are terminal.

## Finality on Solana

For real-money flows, treat `finalized` as the safe-to-act-on signal. `confirmed` is durable enough for most non-adversarial workflows (think: showing a "paid" badge in your dashboard) but a sufficiently motivated cluster reorganization can theoretically roll back a `confirmed` transaction; this does not happen for `finalized` transactions.

Use `confirmed` to release low-stakes side effects (status emails, UI updates) and `finalized` for irreversible side effects (releasing custody, shipping high-value goods, posting to your general ledger).

## Polling cadence

SDP does not currently emit settlement webhooks. Status is observed by polling:

- `GET /v1/payments/transfers/{id}` for a single transfer's current state.
- `GET /v1/payments/transfers?direction=inbound&from=…` for a windowed list — see [Indexing and reconciliation](/docs/payments/accept-indexing).

Cadence depends on how quickly you need to see state transitions and how aggressive your retry budget is. A reasonable starting range:

- **Active checkout** (customer is staring at a payment screen): every 2–5 seconds for up to a minute, then back off.
- **Background reconciliation** (no one is waiting): every 15–30 seconds, or whenever a worker tick fires.
- **Long-tail catch-up** (status reads after the fact): single one-shot reads when your application needs to act, no polling loop at all.

The exact recommended cadence will be tightened in a follow-up once the backend confirms a target; treat the ranges above as defensible defaults today.

## Independent verification

Every transfer that reaches `processing` or beyond carries enough information to verify against the network directly:

- **`signature`** — the Solana transaction signature; paste into [Solscan](https://solscan.io/) or [Solana Explorer](https://explorer.solana.com/) to see the on-chain record.
- **`slot`** — the slot the transaction landed in.
- **`blockTime`** — ISO 8601 timestamp of slot finality.
- **`fee`** — fee paid, in lamports.

If you maintain your own indexer (`getSignatureStatuses` against a Solana RPC), cross-reference SDP's `signature` to your indexer's view to confirm SDP's status reflects what your nodes see.

## Risk metadata

When a risk-screening provider is configured on the organization, transfers may carry a `risk` field with `provider`, `score`, `level` (`low | medium | high | unknown`), and `evaluatedAt`. Use this to gate downstream side effects on a risk threshold; the field is absent when no risk provider is wired up.

Risk evaluation is not blocking by default — a transfer can complete with a high-risk score. If you want a transfer to halt on risk threshold, enforce that in your application logic on top of the `risk.level` value.

## Failure handling

When `status` settles to `failed`:

- Read the `error` field. SDP returns the chain-level error message; common causes are insufficient source funds, account frozen by token authority, or stale blockhash.
- Decide whether to retry. The original transfer record is terminal; a retry creates a new transfer with a new ID and (eventually) a new signature.
- Surface the failure to whoever needs to know — the merchant, the customer, your operations team.

- [Accept overview](/docs/payments/accept-overview) — the broader inbound-payment flow.
- [Indexing and reconciliation](/docs/payments/accept-indexing) — list-based status checking across many transfers.
- [Concepts: the transfer data model](/docs/payments/concepts#the-transfer-data-model) — full field reference.
